# Cūḷahaṁsajātaka (Ja 533)

**ID:** Ja 533
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Cūḷahaṁsajātaka
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0514m.mul4.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷahaṁsajātaka* (Ja 533), titled *The Shorter Tale of the Golden Goose*, is a canonical Pali birth story belonging to the Jātaka collection. According to its traditional frame narrative set at the Bamboo Grove, the Buddha related the tale after the venerable Ānanda offered his life to protect the Buddha when Devadatta unleashed a mad elephant; the Buddha explained that Ānanda had similarly demonstrated unflinching self-sacrifice on his behalf across four past lives [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta is born as a king of golden geese who is captured by a fowler [Anandajoti 2010]. His loyal commander-in-chief, Sumukha, refuses to abandon him despite permission to flee, and both are brought before the human king, who is so impressed by their nobility and virtue that he grants them their release [Anandajoti 2010; Buddhaghosa 1921].

The text is cited in late canonical and commentarial exegesis; for instance, Buddhaghosa’s *Atthasālinī* quotes a verse addressed to Sumukha from the Jātaka to illustrate color classifications and the semantic range of the term *hari* [Buddhaghosa 1921].

**Sources**

- [Anandajoti 2010] Bhikkhu Anandajoti, Buddhist Wisdom Verses (2010) — Summary of the past narrative involving the goose king, commander-in-chief, fowler, and king.
- [Buddhaghosa 1921] Buddhaghosa, The Expositor (Atthasālinī), translated by Pe Maung Tin (PTS, 1921) — Citation of a verse from the Jātaka concerning Sumukha and the explanation of the color term hari.
- [Nyanaponika et al. 2003] Nyanaponika Thera and Hellmuth Hecker, ed. Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha (2003) — Background on Ānanda's willingness to sacrifice his life against Devadatta's elephant as the occasion for the discourse.
